hook_clip: Monday dot com costs a ten-person team one thousand and eighty dollars a year.
outro_clip: The full spec is free at personal software factory dot com. If you build it, tell me what broke. I'm Sam. See you tomorrow.

scenes.text: So can Claude replace it? The spec copies the part of Monday dot com a team uses for its weekly status. One row per project, with an owner and a target date. One square per week, On track, At risk or Blocked. A short note with every update. And a report that writes itself.
cues: On track, At risk or Blocked

scenes.text: The core rule is honesty. Only the project's owner can post its update, and only for the current week. Health is the owner's judgment, and the app never sets it on its own. If an owner misses a week, the square says No update, instead of quietly keeping last week's green. And saving again revises the update. It never adds a second square.

Claude built it in four phases, one prompt each. The foundation. The board, projects and weekly updates. The weekly report. Then reminders and the weekly schedule. After every phase, the acceptance checks ran in a real browser.

Here's what it built. The board shows four projects with a square for each week, and Hiring plan is flagged under Missing updates. On the CRM migration page, Sam revised this week's update from Blocked to At risk, and the activity log kept both. The weekly report assembles itself from the saved updates, with Blocked first. The outbox shows the reminders at nine thirty and the report at three thirty. And on a phone, each project becomes a card with its weekly squares.
In one final run, on a fresh database, all twenty-eight checks passed, along with sixty-four automated tests.

But the more useful result is what broke. The test build exposed six places where Claude had to guess. The reminder promised the report would go out at three, even when there was nobody to send it to. Failed emails were retried forever, with nothing counting the attempts. And an empty report didn't say whether its title and last line stay. Every gap is now fixed in the spec.

Passing every check isn't production-ready. Production sign-in, real email delivery, the hourly job on a real scheduler, hosting, and two people saving the same project at once were never tested. Check those yourself before your team relies on it.

So is it worth building? Monday dot com's Basic plan is nine dollars a seat a month, billed yearly, so ten people pay one thousand and eighty dollars a year. Standard is twelve dollars, and project health across a portfolio is listed only on Enterprise. Build it if every Monday someone rebuilds the same status report. Buy it if you need task boards, Gantt charts, dashboards or automations.
Everything is in one file. The data model, seventeen rules, the seed data, four phase prompts and twenty-eight checks, with all six fixes included.
